The American woodcock (Scolopax minor) initiates incubation following the completion of a clutch of four eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of four eggs], a fixed brood size that appears remarkably conserved across much of the species range. This modest reproductive investment is offset by a single nesting attempt per year [F_R_i = single nesting attempt per year], a strategy that reflects the energetic constraints of exploiting ephemeral, soil-based invertebrate prey during the brief spring window when ground moisture is optimal for foraging. For eggs held under controlled laboratory conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], hatching occurs after an incubation period of approximately 20.5 days [ab = approximately 20.5 days], a developmental duration consistent with the relatively small egg size and the semi-precocial mode of chick development characteristic of scolopacids. Newly emerged precocial chicks weigh only 12 grams [Wwb = 12 grams], a remarkably low neonatal mass that necessitates immediate and intensive parental brooding to maintain thermoregulatory stability. This altricial-like dependency at the point of hatching is somewhat unusual for a shorebird and imposes a heavy energetic burden on the adults during the first few days post-hatch.

Under thermal conditions approaching the species' upper active metabolic range of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the pace of post-hatching development accelerates considerably for the young woodcock. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight capable of evading predators, is attained 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching], a remarkably brief nestling period that typifies many ground-nesting birds that rely on crypsis rather than prolonged parental defense at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This rapid transition to flight capability is matched by an equally fast trajectory toward puberty; gonadal maturation and the onset of gametogenesis are completed by 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching], meaning that young-of-the-year are potentially reproductively active before the end of their first summer at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This accelerated sexual maturation is a key component of the species' compensatory life-history strategy, allowing it to maintain population numbers despite high rates of nest predation and low annual fecundity.

The first successful brood is produced after a markedly longer interval than the age at puberty. Under the same thermoregulatory regime of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the time since birth at first brood is approximately 328.5 days [tR = approximately 328.5 days]. This substantial delay between gonadal readiness and actual breeding reflects the constraints imposed by the species' migratory phenology and the need to acquire sufficient body condition to sustain egg production and incubation. Most female woodcock do not breed until their second calendar year, having returned from migration with ample fat stores. The delay is also influenced by a male-biased adult sex ratio that intensifies competition for display territories; males must establish and defend a singing ground before they can attract a mate, a process that may require multiple seasons for younger, less experienced individuals to successfully accomplish.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a feature common among many scolopacid species. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of 210.5 grams [Wwi = 210.5 grams], whereas males reach a smaller ultimate wet weight of 168.4 grams [Wwi = 168.4 grams]. This 42-gram difference in asymptotic mass is functionally linked to the demands of egg production; the larger female body cavity accommodates the developing clutch and provides a greater absolute lipid reserve for the energetically costly incubation period, during which the female sits motionless on the nest for extended intervals. Males, in contrast, invest heavily in nocturnal singing displays that require sustained muscular exertion rather than large body size, and their leaner frame likely facilitates the rapid, low-level flight maneuvers characteristic of their courtship roding behavior. Field weight data from autumn banding operations consistently corroborate this intersexual divergence in mass.

Neonates emerge with an initial wet weight of 17 grams [Ww0 = 17 grams], which is notably greater than the 12 grams [Wwb = 12 grams] recorded at the moment of hatching for chicks that have not yet fully absorbed the yolk sac. This initial mass reflects the hydrated state of the newly hatched chick before desiccation losses stabilize, and it provides a more accurate baseline for calculating relative growth rates during the first week of life. Maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated at approximately 20.9 years [am = approximately 20.9 years], a figure derived from encounter histories of individuals banded as adults and subsequently recovered during hunting seasons or mortality events at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. Although most woodcock succumb to predation or anthropogenic harvest before reaching advanced ages, this potential lifespan stands in contrast to the species' rapid maturation and low annual reproductive output, illustrating a bet-hedging strategy in which extended individual survival offsets the risk of complete reproductive failure in any single year.
